gloss: A story written to be acted out on a stage.
examples: We saw a *play* about two brothers running a diner.
She has written six *plays*, and three of them were produced.
The *play* runs two hours with one intermission.

gloss: A woman who performs a part in a play, film, or television show.
examples: The *actress* playing the mother is only thirty.
Four *actresses* read for the same part.
She trained as an *actress* before she started directing.
contrast: Many Americans now say *actor* for women too, and reserve *actress* for award categories.

gloss: A section of a play or film that happens in one place and time.
examples: The best *scene* is the argument in the kitchen.
We rehearsed the last two *scenes* all afternoon.
He forgot his lines in the opening *scene*.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *seen*, the past participle of see.

gloss: A main division of a play, or a short self-contained performance.
examples: The first *act* runs almost an hour.
Most modern plays have two *acts* instead of five.
Her comedy *act* is about twenty minutes long.

gloss: A character that an actor plays in a performance.
examples: She landed the *part* of Juliet on her first audition.
He has played small *parts* in a dozen shows.
It is a wonderful *part* for an older actor.

gloss: A play or film meant to be funny and to end happily.
examples: The theater is doing a *comedy* this spring.
He writes dark *comedies* about office life.
It started as a *comedy* and turned very sad in the last act.

gloss: A serious play that ends unhappily for the main character.
examples: Hamlet is the best known *tragedy* in English.
Greek *tragedies* were performed outdoors.
The director staged the *tragedy* in modern dress.

gloss: A play in which the story is carried by songs and dancing.
examples: They took the kids to a *musical* for her birthday.
He knows the words to about forty *musicals*.
The *musical* has been running for eleven years.

gloss: A stage performance that tells a story through formal dancing and music.
examples: We go to the *ballet* every December.
She has danced in twelve different *ballets*.
The *ballet* lasted about ninety minutes.
contrast: The final t is silent, and Americans stress the second syllable: ba-LAY.

gloss: An object an actor carries or uses on stage.
examples: The only *prop* in the whole scene is a coffee cup.
Someone left the *props* on the wrong side of the stage.
That knife is a rubber *prop*, not a real one.

gloss: The scenery and furniture that show where a scene takes place.
examples: The *set* for the second act is a hotel lobby.
They built both *sets* in a week.
The *set* rotates to become the outside of the house.

gloss: A word or signal that tells a performer or technician to do something.
examples: That line is your *cue* to come on stage.
The lighting *cues* are all in the stage manager's book.
He missed his *cue* and came on ten seconds late.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *queue*, a line of waiting people.

gloss: The arrangement of lights used to light a stage or a room.
examples: The *lighting* in the final scene is almost blue.
We spent the whole day working on *lighting*.
Bad *lighting* can ruin a good set.
contrast: Uncountable: say *the lighting was beautiful*, never *the lightings*.

gloss: A lamp that throws a narrow circle of bright light onto one performer.
examples: A single *spotlight* picked her out of the darkness.
Two *spotlights* follow the dancers across the stage.
Step into the *spotlight* when the music starts.

gloss: A large painted cloth hung at the back of a stage.
examples: The *backdrop* is a painted city skyline.
They rolled up both *backdrops* after the show.
A dark blue *backdrop* made the night scene work.

gloss: A person who writes plays.
examples: The *playwright* sat in the back row on opening night.
Three young *playwrights* had work in the festival.
She is a novelist as well as a *playwright*.
contrast: Spelled -wright, like *shipwright*, though it sounds like write and right.

gloss: The person who raises the money for a show and manages the business side.
examples: The *producer* decided to extend the run by a month.
Two *producers* pulled out before rehearsals began.
She works as a *producer* for a small downtown company.

gloss: The words that characters speak to one another in a play or film.
examples: The *dialogue* in the second act feels stiff.
Critics praised the sharp, funny *dialogue*.
She rewrote most of the *dialogue* before opening night.

gloss: A long speech by one character or performer.
examples: He opens the show with a five-minute *monologue*.
Bring two contrasting *monologues* to the audition.
Her *monologue* about her father got a huge reaction.

gloss: A speech in which a character alone on stage says his thoughts aloud.
examples: Everyone knows the *soliloquy* that begins with To be or not to be.
The play has four *soliloquies*, all delivered downstage.
He cut the *soliloquy* down to twenty lines.
contrast: Stress the second syllable: suh-LIL-uh-kwee.

gloss: The moment at the end of a show when the cast comes back on stage to be applauded.
examples: The audience was still clapping through the third *curtain call*.
There were five *curtain calls* on closing night.
She was too sick to take her *curtain call*.

gloss: A full practice performance in costume, just before opening.
examples: The *dress rehearsal* is Thursday at seven.
They ran two *dress rehearsals* because the first one fell apart.
Friends and family can come to the final *dress rehearsal*.

gloss: The place in a theater where tickets are sold.
examples: Pick up your tickets at the *box office* an hour before the show.
Both *box offices* close at eight on show nights.
The *box office* is open from noon on weekdays.

gloss: The first public performance of a show.
examples: Her parents flew in for *opening night*.
He has been through nine *opening nights* and still gets nervous.
*Opening night* was sold out weeks in advance.

gloss: A room backstage where performers change and put on makeup.
examples: Flowers were waiting in her *dressing room*.
The *dressing rooms* are down the hall past the green room.
Four of us shared one tiny *dressing room*.

gloss: The person who runs rehearsals and calls the cues during a performance.
examples: The *stage manager* called places five minutes ago.
Good *stage managers* are worth their weight in gold.
Ask the *stage manager* where your entrance is.

gloss: Sudden fear felt before or while performing in front of people.
examples: He gets terrible *stage fright* before every show.
A little *stage fright* is normal, she told the kids.
She overcame her *stage fright* after about a year.
contrast: Uncountable: *a lot of stage fright*, never *a stage fright*.

gloss: Applause given by an audience that has risen to its feet.
examples: The show got a *standing ovation* on the first night.
Two *standing ovations* in one week is unusual.
The old actor received a long *standing ovation*.

gloss: An actor who learns another actor's part in order to go on if that actor cannot.
examples: The *understudy* went on for the lead last Tuesday.
All three *understudies* rehearse on Monday mornings.
She spent a year as an *understudy* before getting her own role.

gloss: The art or work of performing a part in a play or film.
examples: The *acting* was better than the script deserved.
She has been studying *acting* since high school.
He gave up *acting* and became a teacher.
contrast: Uncountable: *good acting*, never *a good acting*.

gloss: The process of choosing which actors will play which parts.
examples: *Casting* takes about three weeks for a show this size.
The *casting* is the strongest thing about this production.
She does *casting* for two theaters in the city.

gloss: A group of performers who work and travel together.
examples: A small *troupe* from Chicago is performing here all week.
Two dance *troupes* share the theater on weekends.
He joined the *troupe* right out of college.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *troop*, a group of soldiers.

gloss: The bad character in a story or play.
examples: He always gets cast as the *villain*.
The best *villains* think they are doing the right thing.
The *villain* dies at the end of the third act.
contrast: The ending is a weak -uhn, not -AIN: VIL-uhn, and it has no connection to *village*.

gloss: The main female character in a play, film, or book.
examples: The *heroine* leaves home in the very first scene.
Both *heroines* are played by the same actress.
She is a *heroine* you actually want to root for.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *heroin*, the drug.

gloss: The main character, whose story the play follows.
examples: The *protagonist* is a retired boxer with nothing left.
Both *protagonists* are on stage the whole time.
You never really like the *protagonist*, and that is the point.

gloss: The character who works against the main character.
examples: In this version the *antagonist* is the mother.
Strong *antagonists* make a play interesting.
The *antagonist* never raises his voice, which is scarier.

gloss: The actor who plays the most important male part.
examples: Their *leading man* broke his ankle two days before opening.
He played *leading men* for twenty years.
The *leading man* has almost no lines in the last act.
contrast: Irregular plural: *leading men*, not leading mans.

gloss: The actress who plays the most important female part.
examples: The *leading lady* got a bouquet at the curtain call.
Two former *leading ladies* were in the audience.
She was a *leading lady* on Broadway in the sixties.

gloss: A part that is important but smaller than the lead.
examples: He won an award for a *supporting role*.
The best writing in the play is in the *supporting roles*.
She took a *supporting role* just to work with that director.

gloss: The part named in the title of the play or opera.
examples: He is playing the *title role* in Macbeth.
She has sung both *title roles* in that pair of operas.
The *title role* is on stage for almost the entire show.

gloss: A very small acting part with only a few lines.
examples: She started out playing a *bit part* as a waitress.
He took *bit parts* for years before anything bigger came along.
It is a *bit part*, but it gets the biggest laugh.

gloss: A part in which an actor appears on stage but says nothing.
examples: His first job in theater was a *walk-on*.
The crowd scene is played by six *walk-ons*.
It is only a *walk-on*, but you are on stage with the star.

gloss: Someone who takes another performer's place for a time.
examples: They found a *stand-in* two hours before the show.
The *stand-ins* rehearsed while the leads rested.
He worked as a *stand-in* on three different productions.

gloss: A performer whose job is to make people laugh.
examples: The *comedian* did forty minutes without a single note.
Three *comedians* are on the bill tonight.
She is a stand-up *comedian* from Austin.
contrast: Stress moves off the first syllable: KAH-muh-dee for comedy, but kuh-MEE-dee-uhn here.

gloss: Comedy performed alone at a microphone, talking straight to the audience.
examples: He has been doing *stand-up* for six years.
*Stand-up* is harder than it looks.
She got into *stand-up* after college.

gloss: Comic performance made up on the spot, with no script.
examples: She takes an *improv* class on Wednesday nights.
*Improv* teaches you to listen to the other actor.
The show is half scripted and half *improv*.

gloss: A short funny scene performed by a few people.
examples: The fifth graders put on a *skit* about recycling.
The show is built out of a dozen short *skits*.
Their *skit* about the DMV ran long.

gloss: A joke or funny piece of business in a performance.
examples: The falling-ladder *gag* gets a laugh every night.
Half the *gags* in the second act are physical.
It is an old *gag*, but it still works.

gloss: The last words of a joke, where the laugh comes.
examples: He blew the *punchline* and had to start over.
Her *punchlines* land about half a second later than you expect.
Everyone in the room saw the *punchline* coming.

gloss: Someone in the audience who shouts rude things at a performer.
examples: A *heckler* in the back kept yelling at the band.
She handles *hecklers* better than anyone I have seen.
Security walked the *heckler* out after the second warning.

gloss: An evening where anyone who signs up can perform for a few minutes.
examples: There is an *open mic* at the coffee shop on Tuesdays.
He does two or three *open mics* a week.
She tried out her new material at an *open mic*.
contrast: *mic* is short for microphone but is said like *mike*, not to rhyme with pick.

gloss: A performer who entertains people with tricks that look impossible.
examples: They hired a *magician* for the kids' party.
Two *magicians* share the stage in the second half.
The *magician* pulled a card out of my jacket pocket.

gloss: A single act of stage magic that fools the audience.
examples: He learned his first *magic trick* when he was nine.
Some *magic tricks* are three hundred years old.
Do not explain the *magic trick* to the children.

gloss: A performer in funny makeup and costume who does silly things to make people laugh.
examples: A *clown* came out and made balloon animals.
The *clowns* work the crowd between the animal acts.
He trained as a *clown* at a circus school in Florida.

gloss: A performer who does jumps, flips, and balancing feats.
examples: An *acrobat* walked across the stage on her hands.
Six *acrobats* built a human tower.
The *acrobat* landed perfectly and the crowd went crazy.

gloss: A performer who keeps several objects in the air at once.
examples: A *juggler* was working the line outside the theater.
Both *jugglers* used knives in the second half.
The *juggler* kept five clubs going while riding a unicycle.

gloss: A doll moved by hand or by strings to act out a story.
examples: The *puppet* is worked by two people at once.
All the *puppets* were made out of foam and cloth.
She talked to the *puppet* as if it were a person.

gloss: A performer who moves and gives a voice to a puppet.
examples: The *puppeteer* stood in plain sight, dressed in black.
Three *puppeteers* operate the horse.
She has worked as a *puppeteer* since she was twenty.

gloss: A puppet moved from above by strings.
examples: The *marionette* walked across the little stage.
He carves his own *marionettes* out of basswood.
One tangled string can ruin a *marionette*.

gloss: A performance acted out with puppets.
examples: The library puts on a free *puppet show* every Saturday.
The kids sat through two *puppet shows* without moving.
The *puppet show* lasts about half an hour.

gloss: A performer who acts silently, using only movement and facial expression.
examples: A *mime* was working the corner by the fountain.
Two *mimes* opened the show with a short piece.
The *mime* pretended to be trapped in a box.

gloss: Acting without words, using gestures and expressions alone.
examples: The whole opening is done in *pantomime*.
She studied *pantomime* in Paris for two years.
He explained the whole story in *pantomime*.
contrast: In Britain a *pantomime* is also a comic Christmas play for families, a sense Americans do not use.

gloss: A performer who speaks without moving the lips so a dummy seems to talk.
examples: The *ventriloquist* and his dummy closed the first half.
Good *ventriloquists* never let you see the lips move.
She is the only *ventriloquist* I have ever found funny.

gloss: A rope stretched high above the ground for an acrobat to walk on.
examples: She crossed the *tightrope* carrying a long pole.
The two *tightropes* are strung at different heights.
There was no net under the *tightrope*.

gloss: A short bar hung on ropes that acrobats swing from.
examples: He caught her by the wrists as she left the *trapeze*.
Both *trapezes* swing out over the audience.
She has performed on the *trapeze* since she was fourteen.
contrast: Stress the second syllable: tra-PEEZ.

gloss: A difficult or dangerous action performed to impress an audience.
examples: The fall off the balcony is the hardest *stunt* in the show.
All the *stunts* are rehearsed slowly first.
He does his own *stunts*, which makes the insurance people nervous.

gloss: Someone whose job is to perform for an audience.
examples: He was a working *entertainer* for fifty years.
The cruise ship hires a dozen *entertainers* a season.
She is a singer, but really she is an *entertainer*.

gloss: The arrangement of the steps and movements in a dance.
examples: The *choreography* in the ballroom scene is stunning.
She is learning the *choreography* from a video.
New *choreography* was written for this revival.
contrast: Uncountable: *the choreography*, never *the choreographies*.

gloss: The person who creates the dances for a show.
examples: The *choreographer* changed the ending after the preview.
Two *choreographers* worked on the musical.
She started as a dancer and became a *choreographer* at thirty.

gloss: A woman who dances leading roles in ballet.
examples: The *ballerina* held the pose for a full ten seconds.
Three *ballerinas* alternate in the part.
She wanted to be a *ballerina* from the age of four.

gloss: A short stiff skirt that sticks out, worn by ballet dancers.
examples: Her *tutu* had about twelve layers of net.
The *tutus* are hung upside down in the wardrobe room.
He wore a pink *tutu* in the comic number.

gloss: The act or skill of making music with the voice.
examples: The *singing* was the strongest part of the evening.
She has been studying *singing* for three years.
There is more dancing than *singing* in this show.
contrast: Uncountable: *beautiful singing*, never *a singing*.

gloss: How clearly a speaker or singer pronounces words.
examples: His *diction* is so clear you catch every word from the balcony.
The class works on breathing and *diction*.
Her *diction* got sloppy when she rushed.

ru: сила голоса, посыл звука в зал
gloss: The ability to make the voice carry to the back of a hall.
examples: She has wonderful *projection* for such a small person.
We spent the class working on *projection*.
Without a microphone you need real *projection*.

gloss: The sense of exactly when to say or do something for the best effect.
examples: His comic *timing* is perfect.
Good *timing* cannot really be taught.
The *timing* of the blackout was off by a beat.

gloss: A movement of the hands, head, or body that expresses something.
examples: One small *gesture* told us everything about the character.
The director cut half her *gestures* to make the scene simpler.
He made a *gesture* toward the door without looking at it.

gloss: A habit of movement or speech that is typical of a person.
examples: He copied his grandfather's *mannerism* of rubbing his chin.
She built the character out of three small *mannerisms*.
That nervous *mannerism* with the glasses is very funny.

gloss: The quality of holding an audience's attention just by being on stage.
examples: The kid has real *stage presence*.
You can teach technique, but *stage presence* is harder.
She has enormous *stage presence* and a very quiet voice.
contrast: Uncountable: *great stage presence*, never *a great stage presence*.

gloss: A loud whisper meant to be heard by everyone listening.
examples: He said it in a *stage whisper* the whole theater could hear.
Their *stage whispers* got the biggest laugh of the night.
She asked in a *stage whisper* whether it was over yet.

gloss: A remark a character makes to the audience that the other characters do not hear.
examples: He turns and delivers an *aside* right to the front row.
The play is full of *asides* to the audience.
That one *aside* explains the whole plot.

gloss: An instruction printed in a script telling the actors how or where to move.
examples: The *stage direction* just says: he laughs, then stops.
Read the *stage directions* before you learn the lines.
The most famous *stage direction* in Shakespeare involves a bear.

gloss: The planned positions and movements of the actors on stage.
examples: We set the *blocking* for act one this morning.
The *blocking* changes once we get into the real space.
Write your *blocking* in pencil, not pen.

gloss: A particular way of putting a play on stage.
examples: It is a spare, modern *staging* with almost no set.
I have seen four different *stagings* of this opera.
The *staging* puts the audience on three sides.

gloss: A rehearsal where the cast sits and reads the whole script aloud.
examples: The first *read-through* is Monday at ten.
We did two *read-throughs* before anyone stood up.
The *read-through* took three hours with the breaks.

gloss: A rehearsal of a whole show from start to finish without stopping.
examples: We have a *run-through* at four with no costumes.
The last two *run-throughs* went smoothly.
Let us do a quick *run-through* of the fight scene.

gloss: A test performance in which someone competes for a part or place.
examples: *Tryouts* for the school play are Thursday after class.
He drove four hours for a two-minute *tryout*.
She made it through the first *tryout* but not the second.
contrast: American word; the British would usually say *audition* or *trial*.

gloss: A second audition that only some of the actors are invited to.
examples: She got a *callback* for the mother.
*Callbacks* are on Saturday morning.
Three *callbacks* and he still did not get the part.

gloss: A posted list showing which actor is playing which part.
examples: The *cast list* goes up on the door Friday afternoon.
Both *cast lists* are printed in the program.
She read the *cast list* twice before she believed it.

gloss: A large card held off camera or offstage with words for the performer to read.
examples: The host reads most of it off a *cue card*.
Somebody dropped the *cue cards* out of order.
He wrote the whole opening on one *cue card*.

gloss: A person who quietly feeds actors their lines when they forget.
examples: The *prompter* sits just out of sight in the wings.
Old opera houses had *prompters* in a box at the front of the stage.
He froze, and the *prompter* saved him.

gloss: Exercises done before a performance to get the voice and body ready.
examples: The cast does a vocal *warm-up* an hour before curtain.
Her *warm-ups* take about twenty minutes.
Skip the *warm-up* and you will be hoarse by act two.

gloss: A test of the microphones and speakers before an audience comes in.
examples: *Sound check* is at five, doors at seven.
They ran two *sound checks* because of the buzz in the monitors.
Be at the theater in time for the *sound check*.

gloss: A rehearsal that works through the lighting, sound, and scene changes.
examples: The *tech rehearsal* ran until one in the morning.
We have two *tech rehearsals* before we add the costumes.
Nothing is slower than a *tech rehearsal*.

gloss: The moment when the set is changed from one location to another.
examples: The *scene change* has to happen in under thirty seconds.
Music covers the *scene changes*.
That *scene change* needs four people and a rope.

gloss: A change of clothes made by a performer during a show.
examples: She has a forty-second *costume change* in the wings.
There are nine *costume changes* in the second half alone.
The *costume change* takes two dressers.

gloss: Thick oily makeup worn by stage performers.
examples: The dressing room still smells of *greasepaint*.
He wiped the *greasepaint* off with a towel.
Under the lights you need heavier *greasepaint*.
contrast: Uncountable: *some greasepaint*, never *a greasepaint*.

gloss: The person who plans and makes the clothes worn in a production.
examples: The *costume designer* set the whole play in the 1940s.
Two *costume designers* shared the credit.
Ask the *costume designer* before you take that coat home.

gloss: The person who plans how a show will be lit.
examples: The *lighting designer* wanted the whole first act in shadow.
Both *lighting designers* trained at the same school.
The *lighting designer* is up in the balcony with a laptop.

gloss: The art of planning the scenery for a stage production.
examples: The *set design* is the best thing about the production.
She teaches *set design* at the community college.
They cut the budget for *set design* in half.

gloss: A recorded or created noise used in a performance.
examples: The thunder is a *sound effect*, not a real storm.
All the *sound effects* run off one laptop.
That door-slam *sound effect* comes in a beat too late.

gloss: A trick used on stage or screen to make something impossible look real.
examples: The flying is the one big *special effect* in the show.
The *special effects* are simple but they work.
That fire is a *special effect* made of silk and fans.

gloss: A worker who moves scenery and equipment during a show.
examples: A *stagehand* handed her the umbrella in the dark.
Six *stagehands* strike the set in twenty minutes.
He worked as a *stagehand* while he was in school.

gloss: The team of people who handle scenery, props, and equipment backstage.
examples: The *stage crew* wears black so the audience does not see them.
Both *stage crews* were called in for the load-out.
Thank the *stage crew* before you thank anyone else.

gloss: A room where performers wait and relax before going on.
examples: There is coffee and a couch in the *green room*.
The two *green rooms* are on different floors.
We waited in the *green room* for almost an hour.
contrast: The room is not usually green; the name is old and nobody agrees where it came from.

gloss: The side entrance used by performers and crew.
examples: Fans wait by the *stage door* after every show.
The *stage doors* are on the alley behind the building.
She signed programs at the *stage door* for twenty minutes.

gloss: The ropes, pulleys, and bars used to raise and lower scenery and lights.
examples: The *rigging* above the stage is inspected every year.
Do not touch the *rigging* unless you have been trained.
Old theaters still have hemp rope in the *rigging*.
contrast: Uncountable: *the rigging*, never *the riggings*.

gloss: A heavy block used to balance the weight of scenery being flown.
examples: Add another *counterweight* or the drop will fly up too fast.
The *counterweights* are stacked on a steel frame backstage.
One loose *counterweight* is a serious hazard.

gloss: A door in the floor of a stage that a performer can drop through.
examples: The ghost comes up through a *trapdoor*.
There are two *trapdoors* downstage.
Someone left the *trapdoor* open and that is dangerous.

gloss: A loose-woven cloth that looks solid when lit from the front and clear when lit from behind.
examples: The whole dream sequence is played behind a *scrim*.
Both *scrims* fly out before the last scene.
Light the *scrim* from the front and it becomes a wall.

gloss: A row of lights along the front edge of the stage floor.
examples: The old theater still has *footlights* along the apron.
She stepped up to the *footlights* and started to sing.
The *footlights* throw shadows up onto the actors' faces.
contrast: Used only in the plural: *the footlights*, never a footlight.

gloss: A lamp that throws a wide, soft spread of light.
examples: A *floodlight* washes the back wall in amber.
The *floodlights* on the balcony rail cover the whole stage.
Swap the spotlight for a *floodlight* in that scene.
contrast: *flood* rhymes with blood, not with food: FLUD-lyt.

gloss: A control that makes a light brighter or darker.
examples: Bring the *dimmer* down slowly at the end of the scene.
Half the *dimmers* in this board are dead.
The house lights are on a *dimmer*.

gloss: Public attention, from an old kind of bright stage light.
examples: After forty years in the *limelight* she wanted quiet.
He has never been comfortable in the *limelight*.
The younger dancers are stepping into the *limelight* now.
contrast: Uncountable, and almost always used as *in the limelight*.

gloss: The arch or frame through which the audience sees a traditional stage.
examples: The *proscenium* is forty feet wide.
Older *prosceniums* are decorated with gold plasterwork.
They hung a banner across the *proscenium*.

gloss: The sunken area in front of the stage where the musicians play.
examples: Nineteen players are packed into the *orchestra pit*.
Some theaters cover their *orchestra pits* to add seats.
You can see the conductor's head above the *orchestra pit*.

gloss: The lowest balcony level of a theater, above the main floor.
examples: We had seats in the front of the *mezzanine*.
Both *mezzanines* were nearly full.
The *mezzanine* has a better view than the back of the orchestra.
contrast: American theaters say *mezzanine*; British ones call the same level the dress circle.

gloss: A seat in a small separate section at the side of a theater.
examples: Her uncle got us a *box seat* for the opening.
The *box seats* are expensive and the view is sideways.
He watched the whole second act from a *box seat*.

gloss: One of the levels of seating rising above the main floor.
examples: The top *tier* is the cheapest place to sit.
The old opera house has four *tiers* of boxes.
We were on the second *tier*, right over the stage.
contrast: Sounds like *tear* meaning a drop from the eye, not like *tear* meaning to rip.

gloss: A line of seats side by side in a theater.
examples: Our seats are in *row* G, near the middle.
The first three *rows* get splashed in this show.
She stood up and made everyone in the *row* move.
contrast: Here it rhymes with go. The same spelling said /raʊ/, rhyming with cow, means a noisy argument.

gloss: The line of seats closest to the stage.
examples: Never sit in the *front row* at a comedy show.
The *front rows* were held for the producers.
From the *front row* you can hear the actors breathing.

gloss: A seat at the end of a row, next to the walkway.
examples: He always asks for an *aisle seat*.
Both *aisle seats* were already taken.
An *aisle seat* is worth it if you have long legs.
contrast: The s in *aisle* is silent; the word sounds like *I'll*.

gloss: An audience that fills every seat in the theater.
examples: They played to a *full house* on Saturday.
Three *full houses* in a row is a good week.
It is a different show in front of a *full house*.

gloss: Space at the back of a theater for people without seats.
examples: There is *standing room* at the back for twenty dollars.
By seven o'clock only *standing room* was left.
She watched the whole opera from *standing room*.
contrast: Uncountable: *standing room only*, never *a standing room*.

gloss: A performance for which every ticket has been sold.
examples: Friday night was a complete *sellout*.
The tour was a string of *sellouts*.
Nobody expected a *sellout* on a Tuesday.

gloss: A ticket that admits you to every show in a theater's season.
examples: My parents have had a *season ticket* for years.
*Season tickets* go on sale in June.
A *season ticket* works out cheaper than four single seats.

gloss: A small structure where tickets are sold.
examples: There is a discount *ticket booth* in the square.
Two *ticket booths* were open and the line still took an hour.
The *ticket booth* takes cash only.

gloss: The part of a ticket you keep after it has been torn at the door.
examples: Keep your *ticket stub* if you want to come back after intermission.
She saves the *ticket stubs* from every show she sees.
I found an old *ticket stub* in my coat pocket.

gloss: Someone who buys tickets and resells them at a higher price.
examples: A *scalper* outside wanted three hundred dollars a seat.
The *scalpers* work the sidewalk in front of the theater.
Do not buy from a *scalper* unless you like being cheated.
contrast: American word; the British say *ticket tout*.

gloss: A printed program or poster listing the play and its cast.
examples: The *playbill* has a short biography of every actor.
He keeps his old *playbills* in a shoebox.
Read the *playbill* before the lights go down.

ru: козырёк с афишей над входом в театр
gloss: The lit sign over a theater entrance showing what is playing.
examples: Her name is up on the *marquee* in foot-high letters.
The *marquees* along the street were all lit at once.
They changed the *marquee* the day the show closed.
contrast: Stress the last syllable: mar-KEE. In Britain a *marquee* is usually a big tent.

gloss: A person who often goes to see plays.
examples: She is a serious *theatergoer* and sees about thirty shows a year.
*Theatergoers* filled the sidewalk after the curtain came down.
Any *theatergoer* would recognize that opening line.
contrast: American spelling *theater*; the British write theatregoer.

gloss: A performance given to a paying audience before the official opening.
examples: We saw it in *preview*, before the reviews came out.
They cut ten minutes during *previews*.
The first *preview* is a week from Thursday.

gloss: A new production of a play that was performed years earlier.
examples: The *revival* is better than the original production.
There have been four *revivals* since the sixties.
It is a stripped-down *revival* with only six actors.

gloss: The period during which a show is performed regularly.
examples: The play had a six-month *run* downtown.
Both *runs* were extended twice.
The show ends its *run* on the thirtieth.

gloss: A show that is very popular and successful.
examples: Nobody expected the play to be a *hit*.
He wrote two *hits* and a lot of flops.
It was the biggest *hit* of the season.

gloss: A show that fails badly with audiences or critics.
examples: The musical was an expensive *flop*.
Even great directors have *flops*.
It closed after nine performances, a total *flop*.

gloss: The industry of entertainment: theater, film, music, and television.
examples: She has been in *show business* since she was twelve.
*Show business* is not a steady way to pay rent.
He left *show business* and opened a restaurant.
contrast: Uncountable; in speech Americans often shorten it to *show biz*.

gloss: A song or number so good that the audience applauds until the show pauses.
examples: The tap number in act two is the *showstopper*.
The score has two real *showstoppers*.
Her final song is an absolute *showstopper*.

gloss: The best-known performer on a bill, who goes on last.
examples: The *headliner* did not come on until eleven.
Both *headliners* canceled and the show fell apart.
She has been a *headliner* in Las Vegas for a decade.

gloss: The performer who goes on first, before the main attraction.
examples: The *opening act* was better than the band we came for.
Half the crowd talked through both *opening acts*.
He spent two years as an *opening act*.

gloss: The person who introduces the acts and keeps a show moving.
examples: The *master of ceremonies* wore a bright green suit.
Two *masters of ceremonies* split the evening between them.
As *master of ceremonies* he told a joke between every act.
contrast: The plural adds -s to the first word: *masters of ceremonies*. In speech Americans usually say *emcee*.

gloss: The person who chooses what a theater company will perform and sets its style.
examples: The new *artistic director* wants more new plays.
Three *artistic directors* have come and gone in five years.
She was named *artistic director* last spring.

gloss: Someone who helps the director run rehearsals and the production.
examples: The *assistant director* took notes all through the run-through.
Both *assistant directors* were former students of his.
He worked as an *assistant director* on two shows last year.

gloss: A college where people are trained as actors.
examples: She spent three years at *drama school* in New York.
The best *drama schools* take about twenty students a year.
He got into *drama school* on his third try.

gloss: A building where plays are performed.
examples: The old *playhouse* on Main Street is being restored.
Two small *playhouses* share a parking lot.
The *playhouse* seats about four hundred people.

gloss: A large theater built for opera and other big musical productions.
examples: The *opera house* has four tiers of boxes.
Several American *opera houses* were built by mining money.
We had dinner across from the *opera house*.

gloss: A large room or building built for musical performances.
examples: The *concert hall* holds two thousand people.
Both *concert halls* have wonderful acoustics.
They rebuilt the ceiling of the *concert hall* to fix the sound.

gloss: An open-air place with seats rising in curved rows around a stage.
examples: The summer concerts are held in an outdoor *amphitheater*.
Roman *amphitheaters* still stand all over southern Europe.
We spread a blanket on the grass above the *amphitheater*.
contrast: American spelling ends in -theater; the British write amphitheatre.

gloss: A short piece of music or performance between the main parts of a show.
examples: A piano *interlude* covers the scene change.
The two musical *interludes* are the best part of the evening.
The clowns come out during the *interlude*.

gloss: The imaginary wall between the actors and the audience.
examples: She breaks the *fourth wall* and asks the audience a question.
Most realistic plays keep the *fourth wall* firmly in place.
The narrator steps through the *fourth wall* in the first minute.

gloss: A show made of songs, dances, and short comic scenes with no single story.
examples: The theater is doing a *revue* of songs from the thirties.
Small *revues* were once the standard summer program.
It is more of a *revue* than a play.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *review*, the critic's article.

gloss: An older American kind of variety show with singers, comics, and acrobats.
examples: His grandfather worked in *vaudeville* before the movies came in.
*Vaudeville* died out in the 1930s.
The whole number is a tribute to old *vaudeville*.
contrast: Usually said in two syllables, VAWD-vil, with the middle e swallowed.

gloss: A show of songs and comedy performed in a club while the audience sits at tables.
examples: She sings in a *cabaret* on the East Side.
The *cabarets* in that neighborhood stay open until three.
It is an intimate *cabaret* with about forty seats.
contrast: The final t is silent and the stress falls on the last syllable: kab-uh-RAY.

gloss: A line invented on the spot that is not in the script.
examples: That laugh line was an *ad-lib* on opening night.
Half his best *ad-libs* ended up in the final script.
The director hates an *ad-lib* of any kind.
